A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EMI/EMID framework and research study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations across 34 synthetic and 27 natural shifts, correlation analyses, estimator ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds evaluations of newer MLLMs, medical-domain question answering, and instruction tuning with a proposed regularizer in Tables 4–6.

M1.justification: V1 only suggests using the bound for training regularization. V2 introduces and evaluates a concrete objective in Eq. (11): output-entropy-weighted divergences between intermediate visual/text representations and an isotropic Gaussian prior. This extends the retained evaluation framework into a training procedure.

E1.justification: V2 actually evaluates medical image question answering using LLaVA-Med, which v1 mentions only as a motivating example. It also adds instruction-tuning experiments using LLaVA-mix-665K. The original COCO/Wild evaluations, languages, and synthetic perturbation coverage remain.

E2.justification: V2 Table 6 introduces an unregularized LLaVA v1.5 7B instruction-tuning baseline against the regularized variant. Existing MI/JSD estimator comparisons remain unchanged. Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL2.5 are additional evaluation subjects rather than competing evaluation methods.

E3.justification: Definition 2.1 replaces the expected binary win indicator with an expected reward-ratio relative preference score. V2 also evaluates two additional 7B models under synthetic shifts and introduces controlled instruction tuning on a 10% LLaVA-mix-665K subset. Retained numerical results do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The new with/without-regularizer experiment tests its effect on ID performance and visual, textual, and joint-shift robustness. Existing partial-bound analysis, estimator/embedding ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions use Spearman, Kendall, and Pearson correlations with p-values. The additional results follow these existing reporting practices; v2 introduces no repeated-run counts, seed information, or new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V2 Table 4 adds EMI–RP Spearman correlations of 0.767 for Qwen2.5-VL and 0.375 for InternVL2.5. Table 5 adds medical-domain Spearman 0.718 and EMID–bound Pearson 0.930. Table 6 reports regularization comparisons of 65.8→66.3, 68.0→68.3, and 59.6→60.8 for visual, textual, and joint shifts, with ID unchanged at 72.7. Earlier corresponding table values are retained.

T1.justification: Definition 2.1 substantively changes the mathematical judge metric from binary win rate to a reward ratio. Eq. (4) also makes the entropy offset explicit. The EMI/EMID definitions, central theorem statements, assumptions, and appendix proofs remain substantively unchanged; Appendix D.3 mainly adds interpretation and an equivalent chain-rule decomposition.

C1.justification: The introduction and discussion now claim a connection between EMI and relative preference scores instead of discrete win rate. The central claims of introducing EMI and deriving distribution-shift bounds retain their scope.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges loose upper bounds and the absence of a lower bound, and Appendix C.5 requires fixed estimators and embedding models for fair comparisons. It also reframes the partial bound as an EMID predictor rather than a maximum-risk estimate, while Appendix D.3 expands the interpretation of representation capacity and possible applications.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies the entropy approximation and scale-adjusted bound construction underlying the empirical analysis, filling an important implementation gap. V2 also adds a project-code link, identifies perturbation-generation code, and documents the new training subset. These disclosures do not establish a change to the retained experiments' implementation.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations supporting Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2.5, reward-model evaluation, scaling, and transformer approximation arguments, among others. The related-work structure and positioning as an information-theoretic framework for MLLM distribution shifts remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 edits prose and terminology throughout, expands explanatory passages, adds acknowledgements and Appendices C.5/D.3, and updates publication/contact information. The main section sequence and most existing exposition are retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds three compact result tables, relabels preference-score axes in Figures 1 and 6, updates captions including Figure 3's scale-adjustment disclosure, and corrects Table 3's model labels. Existing figures and appendix tables are largely retained, with reflow and renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 broadens validation beyond the LLaVA family and general-domain data, and makes the empirical bound approximation and practical comparison requirements more transparent. These improve applicability and reproducibility. The gains remain limited: the core theoretical proofs are unchanged, and the small regularization gains lack repeated-run uncertainty and detailed training settings.
